newsitem.title: INDIA: Investors wait and watch Indian political twists.
newsitem.headline: Investors wait and watch Indian political twists.

text.p: Foreign investors despondent at India's sudden plunge into political crisis should watch and wait rather than take any drastic decisions, brokers at leading foreign houses in Bombay told Reuters on Monday.

The Congress party's removal of vital support for Prime Minister H.D. Deve Gowda's minority coalition and decision to mount a challenge to form a government spell testing months ahead for investors' confidence.
"I think they should watch and wait to see how this situation plays out," V.V. Sivakumar, head of research at Peregrine Capital India, said.

The turmoil was undoubtedly negative, and manifest in Monday's collapse on Indian stock markets, but it was too early to go into retreat from India, or to take the opportunity of cheap prices to jump in, foreign brokers said.
"It is certainly negative at the moment but I don't expect any strong selling emerging over the next few days," Sivakumar said, adding bargain hunters were also likely to stay away.
There are too many variables in the equation to start tearing up views on India's outlook and investment climate. Now it is time to stand back and weigh fundamentals, analysts said.
Before Congress dropped its bombshell on Sunday, analysts had expected foreign institutional investor inflows to surge to $4.5 billion in calendar 1997 from $3 billion last year.
India's stock markets had been recovering from a two-year slide, and growing confidence in government policies raised hopes that inflows from institutions would accelerate.

Net inflows from institutions -- the only foreign investors allowed to buy stocks in India since it opened up its markets in 1993 -- have totalled $7 billion in that time, just one-third the amount countries like Malaysia and Indonesia have received.

"I don't think anyone should take any drastic decisions on the longer term fundamental outlook for the country," one director of a leading foreign brokerage in Bombay, who requested anonymity, told Reuters.
If the United Front government managed to wean a dissident faction away from Congress to survive the market would be cheered, Sivakumar said.
But an impasse resulting in elections may solve little.
"Elections do not mean an end to the coalition politics we've been having," Sivakumar said.
The worst case scenario would see the country sliding into a protracted political vacuum, delaying vital economic decisions.

A loss of confidence only recently restored by pro-growth, pro-investment budget measures proposed by Finance Minister P.Chidambaram last month, will mean government plans to raise 48 billion rupees in 1997/98 (April-March) through divestment of state shareholdings in companies will be put on hold.
The exchequer will be further injured if investment decisions are deferred, handicapping the economic growth needed to raise revenue to offset proposed sweeping tax cuts.
Brokers were torn over whether elections, if needed, could be called before or after the monsoon (June through September).

The unnamed broker said markets could be encouraged if the crisis was resolved by Congress forming a progressive government with the Tamil Maanila Congress (TMC) -- the party to which Chidambaram belongs.
"If Congress did come inside, with credible leaders and with the TMC on board and if Chidambaram retained the Finance Ministry, it would be taken positively," he said.
Investors will also watch how the Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP), the largest single party in parliament, plays its hand.
Congress support for the coalition had been founded on a mutual desire to keep the Hindu nationalist BJP out of power.
The unnamed broker foresaw the BJP enjoying the collapse of the alliance, but not being in any hurry to precipitate elections or try an early bid to force its way into power.
"After an election who knows," he said.
